contributions.headingText: Sézary syndrome (SS) is a neoplasm of T lymphocytes, defined by the triad of erythroderma; generalized lymphadenopathy; and the presence of clonally related neoplastic T cells with cerebriform nuclei (Sézary cells) in skin, lymph nodes, and peripheral blood.

SS is a generalized disease with a leukaemic presentation and characteristic involvement of the skin, with redness over most of the body (erythroderma). Lymphadenopathy and involvement of any visceral organ can be observed in advanced stages, but the most common sites are the oropharynx, lungs, and CNS. Bone marrow involvement is variable.

SS and mycosis fungoides share overlapping clinical and pathological features but are considered separate entities on the basis of differences in clinical behaviour and cell of origin {15692063}.

Patients present with erythroderma and generalized lymphadenopathy. Other features are pruritus, alopecia, ectropion, palmar or plantar hyperkeratosis, onychodystrophy, and lichenification. Rarely, patients with SS can present with only generalized pruritus {25981000}, and plaques (early stages) and generalized pruritus without erythroderma are rare. An increased prevalence of secondary cutaneous and systemic malignancies has been reported in SS and attributed to the immune dysregulation associated with skewing of the normal T-cell repertoire and loss of normal circulating CD4-positive cells {17224541}.

SS is rare, with a reported incidence of 0.36 cases per 100 000 person-years {33618714} and accounting for 2–3% of all cutaneous T-cell lymphomas {15692063; 30635287}. It occurs in adults, characteristically presenting in patients aged > 60 years, and shows a male predominance {17540844; 15692063}.

Computational studies of large genomic datasets have identified two mutation signatures in treatment-naïve SS, namely signature 1, associated with cellular ageing due to spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosines, and signature 7, characteristic of ultraviolet (UV) irradiation {33597573}. This UV radiation signature is present in circulating tumour cells in SS and has also been found in mycosis fungoides but not in other mature T-cell lymphomas/leukaemias. This indicates that environmental UV radiation exposure is a key causal factor in the transformation of T cells that are either circulating through or resident in skin.

SS cells express markers indicative of a mature T-cell neoplasm, and the putative normal counterparts are circulating central memory T cells (CD27+, CD45RA−, CD45RO+) or skin-homing CD4-positive T cells expressing cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA), CCR4, and CCR7 contrasting with skin-resident memory T cells for mycosis fungoides {20484084}. Patients with SS are immunosuppressed because of the production of type 2 cytokines (Th2), which suppress Th1 immunity. Genomic analyses of SS have revealed complex numerical and structural alterations similar to those in mycosis fungoides {16382449; 12557225; 19843862}. SS is characterized by a high mutation burden reflecting causative UV radiation–induced mutations {33597573}. Recurrent gain-of-function mutations (in PLCG1, CARD11, CD28, CARMIL2 [RLTPR]) {34115827} affect T-cell receptor signalling pathways and upregulate NF-κB activity. Additionally, driver mutations are also found in DNA damage response pathways (in TP53, POT1, ATM), JAK/STAT signalling (STAT5B, JAK3), and chromatin modifiers (ARID1A, TRRAP, DNMT3A, TET2) {11874489; 24497536; 26192916; 26258847; 26415585; 27121473; 26551667; 26551670; 27039262; 31376383; 28694326; 34115827}. Recurrent balanced chromosomal translocations have not been detected, but isochromosome 17q is a recurrent feature of SS {18413736}.

Peripheral blood

Peripheral blood smears reveal characteristic Sézary cells, which are large atypical lymphocytes containing an abnormally shaped, deeply grooved nucleus with nuclear convolutions (cerebriform nucleus).

Lymph nodes and tissues

Involved lymph nodes show partial or complete effacement of architecture by a dense, monotonous infiltrate of Sézary cells {2938724}. The neoplastic cells are medium in size, with irregular contours and deep clefts, and they show CD3 expression.

The cellular infiltrates involving skin tend to be monotonous, and epidermotropism may sometimes be absent. The dermal lymphocytic infiltrate is often perivascular. In as many as one third of biopsies from patients with otherwise classic SS, the histological picture may be nonspecific {9194581}. Bone marrow may be involved, but infiltrates are often sparse and mainly interstitial {12645344}.

Immunophenotype

The neoplastic T cells typically show a CD3+, CD4+, CD8− phenotype, with frequent aberrant loss of pan–T-cell antigens such as CD2, CD5, CD7, and/or CD26 in the neoplastic cells {25864856}. PD1 (CD279) is expressed by neoplastic cells in skin and blood in almost all cases {23247480}. Expression of TOX by tumour cells in the skin has diagnostic value {25777533} and is also of value in lymph node staging, in which it represents a useful tool for identifying tumour cells {33400272}. Sézary cells express CLA and the skin-homing receptor CCR4, as well as CCR7 {17135733}. Sézary cells also typically express TCRαβ, CD25, and ICOS, and sometimes CXCL13. The NK-cell markers KIR3DL2 (CD158k) and NKp46 may also be expressed {16418328; 17703174}.

Differential diagnosis

SS should be distinguished from inflammatory erythrodermic dermatoses and other haematological malignancies presenting with erythroderma. Additionally, SS should be distinguished from adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma. Benign conditions such as drug reactions, psoriasis, chronic eczema, pityriasis rubra pilaris, scabies, dermatomyositis, lupus, pemphigus foliaceus, and erythematous dermatitis should be excluded.
The tumour cells are clonal by TR gene rearrangement {16120144; 1324964; 1654197}.

Essential: (1) erythroderma involving > 80% of the body surface area; (2) evidence of blood involvement by a neoplastic T-cell population defined by clonal TR gene rearrangements; (3) an absolute Sézary cell count ≥ 1000/μL, OR an expanded CD4+ T-cell population with a CD4:CD8 ratio > 10, OR an expanded CD4+ T-cell population with an abnormal phenotype (CD4+/CD7− T cells ≥ 40% or CD4+/CD26− T cells ≥ 30%) {11167693; 16197392; 16204308}.

Staging of SS involves evaluating the skin (T), lymph nodes (N), visceral organs (M), and blood (B). Given the systemic nature of the disease at presentation, patients with SS are considered to have stage IVA1, IVA2, or IVB depending on the presence of nodal and visceral involvement {17540844}.

SS is an aggressive disease, with a median survival time of 32 months and a 5-year overall survival rate of 10–30%, depending on stage {15692063}. Most patients die of an opportunistic infection. The degree of peripheral blood involvement at diagnosis may have an impact on prognosis {17064997}, but the prognostic relevance of bone marrow involvement is unknown.
